info.title: Growth API
info.description: The Growth backend. Every success body is wrapped in `data`, and every error has a `message` and a `requestId`. Signed-in endpoints read the session cookie that Better Auth sets.

servers.description: Local backend. The frontend proxies /api to it.

tags.name: Auth
tags.description: Sign up, sign in and the session. Better Auth serves every path under /api/auth. Only the paths the frontend uses are listed here.

tags.name: Course content
tags.description: Reference data and code snippets. Public.

tags.name: Onboarding
tags.description: The learning style quiz and the answers a new learner gives before reaching the app.

tags.name: Learning path
tags.description: The units and lessons, with the learner's progress.

tags.name: Leaderboard
tags.description: Today's daily challenge, ranked by how fast each learner finished.

tags.name: Lessons
tags.description: Open a lesson, keep a note and mark it started.

tags.name: Tests
tags.description: Lesson tests, checkpoints and the final challenge. An attempt holds up to 5 questions chosen when it starts. The correct answer is only sent after the learner answers.

tags.name: Practice
tags.description: Open-ended practice on one topic. Questions are generated one at a time until the learner stops. Hints and answers use the attempt endpoints. Practice has no stakes: its ratings live only inside the session, so it never changes mastery, difficulty on tests or lesson progress.

tags.name: Daily challenge
tags.description: One generated question a day, the same for everyone. Days start at 00:00 in Africa/Johannesburg. The learner gets one go, timed from when they press Start. No hints, and it never changes mastery or ratings.

lessons.title: What is a binary tree
lessons.summary: Learn the words for a binary tree and the rule that keeps a search tree in order.

lessons.title: Pre-order
lessons.summary: Visit the node first, then its left and right subtrees.

lessons.title: In-order
lessons.summary: Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.

lessons.title: Post-order
lessons.summary: Visit both subtrees first and the node last.

lessons.title: Level-order
lessons.summary: Visit the tree one level at a time, from the top down.

lessons.title: Traversal checkpoint
lessons.summary: A short quiz to check you can tell the four traversals apart.

lessons.title: Height and balance factor
lessons.summary: See why a stick tree is slow and work out each node's height and balance factor.

lessons.title: Single rotations
lessons.summary: Fix a left-left imbalance with a right rotation, and a right-right imbalance with a left rotation.

lessons.title: Double rotations
lessons.summary: Fix a left-right or right-left imbalance with two rotations.

lessons.title: Inserting into an AVL tree
lessons.summary: Insert like in a plain search tree, walk back up updating heights, then fix the first unbalanced node.

lessons.title: Deleting from an AVL tree
lessons.summary: Remove a key in one of three cases, then walk back up and fix every node that went out of balance.

lessons.title: AVL final challenge
lessons.summary: A final quiz that puts insertion, deletion and rotations together.

get.description: Ranks learners by how fast they finished today's daily challenge. Time is whole seconds after 00:00 South African time, and ties share a rank. The top 10 only includes learners who chose to appear. The signed-in learner's own entry is separate, and is hidden with no rank when they opted out.

lesson.title: In-order
lesson.summary: Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
lesson.notePrompt: Explain in-order in your own words. Why does in-order give the keys of a search tree from smallest to biggest?
objectives: List the nodes of a tree in in-order
Say how the in-order code differs from the pre-order code
Trace the recursive in-order code and say which calls wait on the call stack
Explain why the in-order of a search tree gives its keys in sorted order

body.markdown:
## The in-order rule

In-order also starts at the root, but the steps are in a different order:

1. Do in-order on the left subtree.
2. Visit the node.
3. Do in-order on the right subtree.

## The code

```
inorder(node):
  if node is empty: return
  inorder(node.left)
  visit(node)
  inorder(node.right)
```

This is similar to the pre-order code with `visit(node)` on line 4 instead of line 3.

coreBlock.transcript: The in-order rule. In-order also starts at the root, but the steps are in a different order. One, do in-order on the left subtree. Two, visit the node. Three, do in-order on the right subtree. The code. Line 1: inorder of node. Line 2: if node is empty, return. Line 3: inorder of node dot left. Line 4: visit node. Line 5: inorder of node dot right. This is similar to the pre-order code with visit node on line 4 instead of line 3.

styleBlock.transcript: The code runs on a tree with 8 at the root, 4 on the left and 12 on the right. inorder(8) calls inorder(4) at line 3 and waits on the stack. 4 has no children, so inorder(4) visits 4 and returns. inorder(8) carries on at line 4 and visits 8, then calls inorder(12) at line 5, which visits 12. The visited list is 4, 8, 12.

body.markdown:
## Say the new rhythm

Pre-order was "me, left, right". In-order moves _me_ to the middle: **left, me, right.**

Say it out loud a few times. The node waits until its whole left side is done.

otherBlocks.transcript: Say the new rhythm. Pre-order was "me, left, right". In-order moves me to the middle: left, me, right. Say it out loud a few times. The node waits until its whole left side is done.

body.instructions: Use the rule: tap the left side, then the node, then the right side.

otherBlocks.transcript: A tree with 20 at the root. 10 is on its left. 30 is on its right. Use the rule: tap the left side, then the node, then the right side. The answer is 10, 20, 30.

body.markdown:
## Write the lines that run

Write down each line of the code that runs on this tree, in order, starting with `inorder(8)`. Leave out the checks for empty nodes.

otherBlocks.transcript: Write the lines that run. The tree has 8 at the root, with 4 on its left and 12 on its right. 4 has children 2 and 6. Write down each line of the code that runs on this tree, in order, starting with inorder of 8. Leave out the checks for empty nodes.

body.markdown:
## Trace a small tree

Press **Step** to run the code on the tree one line at a time.

Watch the call stack. `inorder(20)` can't visit 20 until `inorder(10)` is done, so it waits on the stack.

coreBlock.transcript: Trace a small tree. Press Step to run the code on the tree one line at a time. Watch the call stack. inorder(20) can't visit 20 until inorder(10) is done, so it waits on the stack. The code runs on a tree with 20 at the root, 10 on the left and 30 on the right. inorder(20) calls inorder(10) first, and waits at line 3. 10 has no children, so inorder(10) visits 10 and returns. Then inorder(20) visits 20 at line 4, and calls inorder(30) at line 5, which visits 30. The visited list is 10, 20, 30.

body.markdown:
## Hear the wait

Say each visit as it happens: "10 ... 20 ... 30."

There's a long wait before you hear 20. inorder(20) sits on the stack the whole time 10 is being done.

otherBlocks.transcript: Hear the wait. Say each visit as it happens: "10 ... 20 ... 30." There's a long wait before you hear 20. inorder(20) sits on the stack the whole time 10 is being done.

body.markdown:
## Make a card pile

Write `inorder(20)`, `inorder(10)` and `inorder(30)` on three scraps of paper.

As you press **Step**, put a card on the pile when its call starts, and take the top card off when it finishes.

otherBlocks.transcript: Make a card pile. Write inorder of 20, inorder of 10 and inorder of 30 on three scraps of paper. As you press Step, put a card on the pile when its call starts, and take the top card off when it finishes.

body.markdown:
## Write the stack

Write down the call stack, top first, each time a call starts or finishes on this tree. Leave out the calls on empty nodes.

otherBlocks.transcript: Write the stack. The tree has 40 at the root, with 20 on its left and 60 on its right. 20 has 10 on its left. Write down the call stack, top first, each time a call starts or finishes on this tree. Leave out the calls on empty nodes.

body.markdown:
## Trace the bigger tree

8 is the root, but it isn't visited first. The code finishes the whole left subtree, 2, 4 and 6, before it visits 8.

coreBlock.transcript: Trace the bigger tree. 8 is the root, but it isn't visited first. The code finishes the whole left subtree, 2, 4 and 6, before it visits 8. The code runs on the tree with 8 at the root. It goes left until it reaches 2, which it visits first. Then it visits 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14. While the left subtree runs, inorder(8) waits on the stack at line 3.

otherBlocks.transcript: A tree with 50 at the root. 30 is on its left, with children 20 and 40. 70 is on its right, with children 60 and 80. Tap the nodes in in-order. The answer is 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80.

body.markdown:
## Predict first

Write the in-order before you step. Hint: find the leftmost node and start there.

Tick each key as the trace visits it.

otherBlocks.transcript: Predict first. Write the in-order before you step. Hint: find the leftmost node and start there. Tick each key as the trace visits it.

body.markdown:
## Ascending order

In a binary search tree, everything on the left is smaller than everything on the right. In-order traversal will produce the ascending order of the keys in the tree.

coreBlock.transcript: Ascending order. In a binary search tree, everything on the left is smaller than everything on the right. In-order traversal will produce the ascending order of the keys in the tree.

styleBlock.transcript: The code runs on a tree with 40 at the root. 20 is on its left, with children 10 and 30. 60 is on its right, with 50 on its left. Step through and watch the visited list: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Each key is bigger than the one before it.

body.markdown:
## Hear it count up

Read the in-order out loud: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. You can hear it count up. 

In a binary search tree, in-order always gives the keys smallest to largest.

otherBlocks.transcript: Hear it count up. Read the in-order out loud: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. You can hear it count up. In a binary search tree, in-order always gives the keys smallest to largest.

body.instructions: Tap the keys from smallest to biggest. That's the in-order.

otherBlocks.transcript: A tree with 44 at the root. 22 is on its left, with children 11 and 33. 66 is on its right, with children 55 and 77. Tap the keys from smallest to biggest. That's the in-order. The answer is 11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77.

body.markdown:
## Why it's sorted

Fill in the gaps in your notes:

- Everything in a node's left subtree is ___ than the node.
- Everything in its right subtree is ___.
- In-order visits left, then the node, then right, so the keys come out ___.

otherBlocks.transcript: Why it's sorted. Fill in the gaps in your notes. Everything in a node's left subtree is blank than the node. Everything in its right subtree is blank. In-order visits left, then the node, then right, so the keys come out blank.

coreBlock.transcript: A tree with 36 at the root. 18 is on its left, with 9 below it. 64 is on its right, with children 52 and 71. Tap the nodes in in-order. The answer is 9, 18, 36, 52, 64, 71.

post.description: Starts a lesson test, or a checkpoint test for a checkpoint. Locked lessons can be tested, so a learner can test out of them. If the learner already has an unfinished attempt for the lesson, that one is returned with 200. Two starts at the same moment make one attempt. A lesson with no questions returns 409.

post.description: Each hint lowers the score for that answer. Works in practice attempts too. Returns 409 when the question is not the current one, is already answered, has no hints left, or the attempt is finished.

data.hint: In-order traversal visits the left subtree first, then the node, then its right subtree.

post.description: Grades the answer, updates the learner's rating for the question's lesson and returns the correct answer and the explanation. After the last answer of a test, `question` is null and `result` is set. In practice `result` is always null and the next question comes from the practice questions endpoint. A pass completes the lesson and every lesson before it. The answer type must match the question type. A question id that is not in the attempt returns 404. A question that is already answered, is not the current one, or an attempt that is finished returns 409.

200.description: The feedback, and the next question or the result.

get.description: A topic is available when an unlocked lesson has generated questions for it. Unavailable topics return 409 from the start endpoint.

200.description: Every topic and whether it can be started.

post.description: Always starts a new attempt and finishes any unfinished practice attempt first. Questions come from lessons the learner has unlocked. The rating for each lesson starts at the learner's stored rating and then changes inside the session only, and difficulty follows it. A topic with no questions returns 409.

question.prompt: Put the keys of this tree in the order a pre-order traversal visits them.

post.description: Finishes the attempt and returns the summary: questions answered, how many were right and the rating change for each lesson (rating before and after, inside the session). An unanswered question is dropped. Finishing twice returns the same summary.

get.description: The first request of the day creates the day's challenge. Returns whether the learner has started or finished it, the question while it is in progress, and the result once it is answered. Never starts the clock.

post.description: Starts the clock and returns the question without its answer. Starting again returns the same attempt with 200, so a double click or a reload can't restart the clock.

200.description: It was already started or finished.

post.description: Grades the answer, stops the clock and returns the result with the correct answer and the explanation. Answering before starting, or a second time, returns 409. A question id that isn't today's returns 404.
